role: Analysis module: computes the old-against-new statistics, writes sections 0-3 and 7 of FACTS.md.
purpose: `render(D)` takes the interval records that `build_facts.py` collected from the raw result files, and it returns the verdict object for facts.json and the complete text of the facts sheet `S/FACTS.md`. This file computes the old-against-new pairs, medians, drops and ranges. It writes the title, sections 0 to 3 and section 7 itself, and it calls facts_text4.py for sections 4 to 6.

main_flow.step: `build_facts.py` imports this module. The import sets the fixed texts and three constants with the names of earlier 8000 MT/s data sets (`BW12`, `BW11`, `BWX`).
`build_facts.py` calls `render(D)`. `render` calls `analyse(D)` and `register(D)`, and it creates the verdict object `V` and the empty line list `L`.
`analyse` builds the 6 pairs of part A. For each session (1 to 3) and each round (1, 2) it takes the 3 intervals of `bw_old read` and of `bw_new read`, the two medians, their ratio and the drop.

`analyse` builds the pairs of five bwx12 data sets with `pairs`. One pair holds the oldread interval and the asmread interval of the same process and round, with the drop between them. A pair of part C also holds the `read` interval and its drop.
`analyse` defines `pool`. It selects the records of several data sets for one kernel and, when given, one position.
`register` gives every script, raw file and external source a reference number for the file list of section 7.

`render` reads values that several sections use: the two interval lengths (`secA`, `secX`), the buffer size, the start and end times of go.sh and go2.sh, and the time of the rules file. Guards check that the rules file is older than the run.

`render` puts the drops of the pairs of the five 7200 MT/s data sets into six lists (`dl`, `di`, `df`, `dcr`, `dca`, `dpa`). The drops of the two L-1 pairs enter no list. A guard stops the script unless every drop of the six lists is above 0. A drop above 0 means that the new side is below the old read kernel. A second guard checks for every pair of part A that the highest `bw_new read` interval is below the lowest `bw_old read` interval.
`render` splits the read and asmread intervals of part C into five groups by the kernel that ran directly before (`cgroup`).
`render` selects the record lists for Q2 and compares 8 pairs of ranges, 7200 MT/s against 8000 MT/s, with `compare`.
`render` compares the load-only kernels of part A, session 1, with the 8000 MT/s range of the same round (list `pa3`).
It writes the title and the notes under the title.

It writes the heading of section 0. Guards check the patterns that the Short version states. The index `i_short` remembers the place for the Short version. The function `short_version` is defined here and runs later (step 26).
It writes the word list, the request text and the questions Q1 and Q2.
Section 1.1: the table of the steps of the run with their times and gaps.
Section 1.2: the table of the state lines, and the proof of the boot, the module count and the memory speed.
Section 1.3: the system load at every launch.
Section 1.4: the list of the integrity checks that `build_facts.py` ran.
Section 1.5: the differences between the procedure of 2026-11-13 and part A, the Linux settings compared between the two boots, and what the saved files show about the firmware settings.
Section 2: the decisions (a) to (r).

Section 3.1, part A: one table row per process of `read` and `asmread` with the 3 interval rates and their median (24 of the 72 processes of part A), then one row per pair with the ratio and the drop.
Section 3.2, parts L and I and the earlier run F72d12: one table row per pair with the oldread rate, the asmread rate and the drop.
Section 3.3, part C: one table row per process and round, then one row per group with its range and its drops.
Section 3.4: the table of the smallest and the largest drop per part or group, and the verdict text for Q1 (`V['q1']`).

It calls `section4` of facts_text4.py. That function appends sections 4, 5 and 6 to `L`, adds the rows of `V['q2_rows']` (36 of the 42 rows through `q2row`, line 359), and sets the verdict for Q2 [Ref3] [Ref6].
It calls `short_version` and inserts the three sentences and the detail list at the index `i_short`, which is inside section 0.

Section 7: the file list. A guard checks that every path in the list `OPENED` of facts_data.py is in the file list. `OPENED` holds the files that were opened with the function `_open`, and the paths that `build_facts.py` added [Ref1] [Ref2].
It joins the lines to one text, checks the date rule with `check_dates`, and returns `V` and the text.
`build_facts.py` then writes `V` into facts.json and the text into `S/FACTS.md` [Ref1].

behavior_notes: **A module, not a program.** The file has no `main` function. `build_facts.py` imports it and calls `render(D)` once [Ref1]. This file prints nothing and writes no file. `build_facts.py` writes facts.json and `S/FACTS.md` after `render` returns.

**From a raw row to a printed rate.** Step 1: the benchmark writes the rows of one interval into a csv file. Step 2: facts_data.py reads the rows, and build_facts.py stores the rate of the interval in the field `GBps` of one record [Ref1] [Ref2]. Step 3: this file selects records with `sel` and groups them. It takes the median of the 3 intervals of a part A process, or the lowest and the highest value of a list (a range). A drop of a bwx12 pair is computed from the rates of two single intervals as the records hold them (statistic 2). Step 4: `g` prints the value with 2 decimals. This file computes no mean, and it adds no rates of different processes or sessions.

**No result csv is read here.** Each rate is already in a record of `D['recs']` when `render` starts. Part A: the field `GBps` is the value of column 7 (`aggregate_GBps`) of one interval row of `threads120.csv`. The benchmark printed that value. The header line of the csv gives its formula: the sum of the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest elapsed time of a thread [Ref7]. The 8000 MT/s data sets A-2 and A-3 come from the files `A1.csv` and `A3.csv` [Ref1]. The interval rows of these files have the same columns. bwx runners: facts_data.py computes `GBps`. For each T row of the interval (one row per thread) it divides `bytes` (column 7) by `elapsed_s` (column 8) and by 1e9. Then it adds the values of all threads [Ref1] [Ref2] [Ref8]. This file adds no bytes and no thread rates. The only files that this file opens are the rules file, `ra.sh` and the DIMM report. It reads a time from the rules file and two numbers from `ra.sh` (the limit of runnable tasks and the sleep time in seconds). Guards check that the rules file and the DIMM report hold certain sentences. It takes no rate from these files.

**Rows that never become a record.** The row `best` of each part A process is not an interval, and facts_data.py skips it. `A1.csv` and `A3.csv` also hold one row per thread and interval, with the first field `thread`. No record takes its rate from these rows [Ref2]. `A3.csv` holds 12 processes. Only the 3 processes with the tags `onebuf-ms500-1` to `onebuf-ms500-3` become records (data set A-3). `build_facts.py` uses only the header lines of the processes in four more csv files of bw_old and bw_new runs: `one-thread.csv` of the run of 2026-11-13, `A2.csv`, and `A5.csv` and `A6.csv` of the folder `partA-20261113T204939Z`. No record comes from these four files [Ref1]. A folder of an earlier bwx run can hold more csv files than its data set uses. Only the files that a list in `build_facts.py` names become records, for example `a6456.csv` out of the 5 csv files in the folder of L-1 [Ref1]. For L-1 to L-4 these are the files that the rules file lists [Ref5]. From the earlier data sets L-2 to L-4, R0 and R0b only oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1 become records. From the data sets of the first runner bwx only the kernels oldread, read and asmread become records [Ref1] [Ref2]. The csv files of these data sets also hold more processes than the data sets use. Only the processes whose tag starts with `common-6000-` become records of B7a, B7b, C3a and C3b [Ref1]. These are 8 of the 48 processes of each file `B7.csv` and 4 of the 18 processes of each file `C3.csv` [Ref11]. The I row of a bwx interval holds a second rate in its column `aggregate_GBps`: the bytes of all threads divided by the longest elapsed time of a thread [Ref8]. No record takes its rate from the I row [Ref1] [Ref2]. The integrity check `I-agg` compares that value with the rate from the T rows. It covers the 9 bwx12 files of the rerun only. It passes when every difference is below 0.05 GB/s [Ref1].

**Rates that this file does not use.** The statistics of this file use `read` and `asmread` of part A, `oldread` and `asmread` of part L, control I and F72d12, and `oldread`, `read` and `asmread` of part C. This file computes no statistic from the rates of write, copy, asmwrite and asmcopy (part A) or of read_nop96, read_nop256 and read_1pl (part L, control I, F72d12 and L-1). No interval is dropped as a warm-up interval. No outlier is removed. Every selected interval enters its median or its range.

**Statistic 1: the pairs of part A (lines 288 to 301).** There is one pair per session (1, 2, 3) and round (1, 2). That gives 6 pairs. Each side is one process with exactly 3 intervals, and a guard checks this count. The two processes of a pair ran directly one after the other. In round 1 `bw_old read` is process 1 of part A in its session, and `bw_new read` is process 2. In round 2 `bw_new read` is process 23, and `bw_old read` is process 24, the last one [Ref6]. `old_med` and `new_med` are the medians of the 3 rates of `bw_old read` and of `bw_new read`. `ratio` = `new_med / old_med`. `drop` = `(1 - ratio) x 100`, in percent. `ratio_lo` = lowest bw_new interval / highest bw_old interval. `ratio_hi` = highest bw_new interval / lowest bw_old interval. `ao_ratio` and `an_ratio` are the medians of `bw_old asmread` and of `bw_new asmread`, each divided by `old_med`.

**Statistic 2: the pairs of bwx12 (lines 303 to 321).** For each process (`tag`) of a data set and for each round (0, 1), `pairs` takes the one oldread record and the one record of each named kernel. `drop_<kernel>` = `(1 - GBps of that kernel / GBps of oldread) x 100`, in percent. No median is taken here: a pair uses two single intervals of the same process and round. The named kernel is asmread for `rerun-L`, `control-I`, `F72d12` and `L-1`. The named kernels are read and asmread for `rerun-C`. In a crev process of part C, oldread is the last kernel of each round (position 2). So a pair of a crev process compares read and asmread with an oldread interval that ran after them.

**Statistic 3: the groups of part C (lines 399 to 411).** `cgroup` selects the part C records with one kernel and one `kernel_before`. The five groups are: read after oldread, read after asmread, asmread after read, asmread as the first interval, asmread after oldread. Each group keeps its records and their drops from statistic 2. A guard checks that the five groups together hold every read and asmread interval of part C. The facts sheet gives no range over all read intervals or over all asmread intervals of part C. `render` computes the range of all read intervals of part C once (`gC`, line 1399). No later line reads it.

**Statistic 4: the range comparisons for Q2 (lines 413 to 425).** `compare` is called 8 times. Six calls compare oldread and asmread of part L, of control I and of F72d12 with the pool of the data sets L-1 to L-4 (oldread at position 0, asmread at position 1). One call compares `bw_old read` of part A with `bw_old read` of the data sets A-1 to A-3. In part A, in A-1 and in A-2, `bw_old read` of round 1 is the first process of its csv file, and `bw_old read` of round 2 is the last process [Ref6]. A-3 holds 3 processes of `bw_old read`, and other processes of `A3.csv` ran between them [Ref6]. One call compares oldread of part C with the oldread pool. The part C list holds oldread at position 0 (cfwd) and at position 2 (crev). The pool holds oldread at position 0 only. The oldread pool and the asmread pool each hold intervals of two lengths: 6 s in L-1 (2 of the 11 intervals) and 4 s in L-2 to L-4 (9 of the 11 intervals) [Ref6]. Part L, part C, control I and F72d12 hold intervals of 6 s only [Ref6]. Each call returns both min-to-max ranges, the result of the overlap test, the distance of the nearest ends, the wording and the width of the 8000 MT/s range.

**The overlap test.** Two ranges overlap when `a.lo <= b.hi` and `b.lo <= a.hi` [Ref2]. So two ranges that only touch at one end count as overlapping. `compare` sets the wording to `SAME` when they overlap and to `DIFFERS` when they do not. The distance is positive when the 7200 MT/s range lies above the 8000 MT/s range, negative when it lies below, and 0 when the ranges overlap.

**Statistic 5: the load-only kernels of part A, session 1 (lines 427 to 439).** For `bw_new read`, `bw_new asmread` and `bw_old asmread`, and for each round, the 3 intervals of session 1 are compared with the range of the data sets A-1 and A-2 of the same round. The result holds the distance in GB/s of each interval that lies above or below that range, and the count of the intervals inside it. The data set A-2 holds no process of `bw_old asmread`. So for that kernel the 8000 MT/s range comes from the 3 intervals of A-1 alone [Ref6]. A-1 has the process order of part A. A-2 ran its 12 processes in another order. For example, `bw_new read` of round 2 follows `bw_old write` in part A and in A-1 (process 23 of 24). In A-2 it follows `bw_new asmread` (process 11 of 12) [Ref6]. facts_text4.py prints the 6 results in section 4.3 of the facts sheet and appends them to `V['q2_rows']` [Ref3].

**More ranges over several data sets together.** Besides statistics 4 and 5, three lines take the lowest and the highest `GBps` of a list that joins the records of several data sets (`rng`). Line 1138: `bw_old read` of the data sets A-1 and A-2 together (12 intervals of 4 processes), for the text that rule F1 point 5 requires. Line 1451: oldread over part L, control I and F72d12 together (12 intervals of 6 processes), and asmread over the same processes. The bullet after the verdict of section 3.4 prints the distance between the two ends of each of these two ranges. Line 542: the same asmread range, for a detail line of section 0. `short_version` also counts the `bw_old read` intervals of part A that lie below and above the 8000 MT/s range (lines 481 and 482).

**Verdicts set in this file.** `V['q1']` (line 1433) is the answer text for Q1. Its percent values come from `pcr`. Each call of `pcr` gives the lowest and the highest drop of one list. The lists are the two read groups of part C, `dl`, `dpa`, the three asmread groups of part C, `di` and `df`. The Q1 sentence of the Short version (line 489) quotes the two read groups of part C only. `V['q1_parts']` (line 1426) holds 9 entries, one per part or group, each with the smallest and the largest drop in percent [Ref6]. `V['short_version']` (line 559) holds the three sentences and the detail list of section 0. `V['rule_wordings']` (line 345) holds the three fixed wordings. `q2row` (line 359) appends one comparison row to `V['q2_rows']` per call, and only facts_text4.py calls it. facts_text4.py appends the 6 rows of statistic 5 without `q2row` [Ref3]. facts_text4.py sets `V['q2']`, `V['insufficient_data']`, `V['hypotheses']` and the other entries [Ref3].

**The answer words are fixed text.** The word "Yes" of `V['q1']` and sentences such as "still below" are written in the templates. They are not chosen by an `if`. Guards before them check that the data show the stated pattern. The file holds 66 calls of `need`. When one fails, `need` raises `SystemExit`, `render` does not return, and `build_facts.py` writes neither facts.json nor FACTS.md [Ref1].

**A failed integrity check.** Section 1.4 prints `pass` or `FAILED` for each integrity check (line 921). This file has no guard on the result of a check. A guard in `section4` of facts_text4.py stops the script when a check failed [Ref3]. So a facts sheet that was written shows `pass` for every check.

**Rounding.** Every statistic is computed from the `GBps` values as the records hold them. Rounding happens only where a value is printed or stored in `V`. `g` prints a rate with 2 decimals (0.01 GB/s) and `pc` prints a percent value with 1 decimal, both half up. Their helper `_q` first rounds to 6 decimals, which removes the small errors of binary floating-point numbers. Ratios are printed with `%.3f` and loads with `%.2f`, which use the rounding of Python. In `V`, the drops are rounded with `round(x, 2)` and the distances with `round(x, 3)`. `build_facts.py` rounds every floating-point number of `V` to 3 decimals when it writes facts.json [Ref1]. The part A csv prints `aggregate_GBps` with 2 decimals, so a part A rate has 2 decimals from the start [Ref7].

**The Short version of section 0 is built after section 6.** The third sentence of the Short version and 4 of its 12 detail lines quote values that `section4` computes. So `render` remembers the index `i_short` (line 474), runs `section4` (line 1464) and then inserts the result of `short_version` at that index (line 1467).

**Sections of S/FACTS.md that this file writes.** The title with its notes. Section 0 (Short version, the word list, the request, Q1 and Q2). Section 1 (run record, 1.1 to 1.5). Section 2 (decisions). Section 3 (Q1: old against new at 7200 MT/s, 3.1 to 3.4). Section 7 (files). Sections 4, 5 and 6 come from `section4` of facts_text4.py, which appends to the same list `L` [Ref3] [Ref4].

**Import inside `render`.** facts_text4.py imports helper functions from this file in its first lines [Ref3]. This file imports `section4` inside `render` (line 1458), not at the top. An import at the top of both files makes Python raise an `ImportError` (checked with two test files of the same layout).

**The pattern `(need(...), value)[1]`.** The lambdas `one` (line 286), `one_len` (line 372) and `one_set` (line 1063) build a tuple of two items and return the second. Python evaluates the first item, the guard, before it returns the value.

**Global state.** `OTHER_DAY` is a set at module level. `hmd` adds each time of day that it prints for a day other than 2026-11-17. `render` empties the set at its start (line 357). `check_dates` uses it at the end to find a time of another day that is printed without its date.
**Reference numbers follow the call order.** In `register` a file gets its number at its first `a(...)` call. So the order of these calls fixes the numbers `[RefN]` in the facts sheet.

**What the guard of the file list covers.** The guard in line 1475 tests the paths in the list `OPENED` of facts_data.py. `_open` of facts_data.py adds each file that it opens to this list, and `build_facts.py` adds some paths itself [Ref1] [Ref2]. stat_bwx.py opens files without `_open`. So it adds no path to the list. For the integrity check `x-bwx`, stat_bwx.py reads every csv file of each folder that the check passes to it [Ref1] [Ref10]. So one run of `build_facts.py` also reads 35 csv files in the folders of earlier bwx runs that the file list does not name. An example is `a0001.csv` in the folder of L-1. No record comes from these 35 files.

**A result that is not read.** `N['p80']` (line 321) holds the pairs of the 8000 MT/s data set `L-1`. No line of facts_text.py or facts_text4.py reads it. The call still runs the guard of `one` for that data set.

words.def: the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17 at 7200 MT/s: the runs of the scripts go.sh and go2.sh.

the run scripts. go.sh is the driver script of the rerun: it runs three sessions and then one more part C process. go2.sh is the script of control I. ra.sh is the script of part A: it starts the 24 processes of bw_old and bw_new one after the other. rx.sh is the runner script of the bwx12 processes (parts L, C and I): it starts one process per line of a spec file. r0.sh is the earlier script that ran the two bwx11 processes of the data set R0.

`S` is the folder of this script (`/home/jhan/workspace/titan/cache-perf/crb/tmp/agent-scratch/w120-7200-2026-11-17`). `R` is the folder `/home/jhan/workspace/titan/cache-perf/crb/results`. It holds the result folders that were copied back from CRB.

the file `S/FACTS.md`. `render` of this file builds its text, and `build_facts.py` writes the file. It holds the numbers of the rerun, and its section 7 lists the raw files that they come from. Its first lines call it the source for the report of the rerun. The report script make_report.py computes its numbers from the records of facts.json and compares them with the facts sheet [Ref9].
the second output file. It holds every record of `D['recs']` (one record per collected interval), plus the parts `meta` and `verdicts`. `build_facts.py` writes it.

the two questions of the facts sheet. Q1: at 7200 MT/s with 12 memory modules, is the whole-chip read rate of the new read kernel still below that of the old read kernel, and by how much. Q2: did either kernel's rate differ from the earlier runs with 12 modules at 8000 MT/s.

the data object, a Python dictionary. The functions `collect` and `run_checks` of `build_facts.py` fill it from the raw files [Ref1]. This file only reads it. Keys used here: `recs` (the records), `checks` (the integrity checks), `A` (the 3 part A folders), `X` (the 9 bwx12 folders of the rerun), `events` (the steps of the run in time order), `logs` (the logs of go.sh and go2.sh), `P_kB` (the buffer sizes in kB in the P rows of the rerun), `base`, `rx` and `step` (earlier runs), `env_partA` (the text of env.txt of the run folder of A-2), and `try6`, `probe13`, `mod`, `fw`, `a2pre`, `boot_table` (records of the machine state).

one dictionary per timed interval, in the list `D['recs']`. The statistics use these fields: `dataset`, `binary`, `kernel`, `session`, `round`, `pos` (the position), `interval`, `tag`, `kernel_before`, `proc_key`, `boot`, `GBps`, `mesh0_GBps`, `mesh1_GBps`, `passes`, `min_ms`.

the rate of one interval in GB/s, with GB = 1e9 bytes. It is set before this file runs. Part A: the value of the column `aggregate_GBps` of the interval row in `threads120.csv`. The records of the data sets A-2 and A-3 take it from `A1.csv` and `A3.csv`. bwx runners: the sum over the T rows of the interval (one row per thread) of `bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9` [Ref1] [Ref2].
bwx records only: the same sum as `GBps`, taken over the threads on CPUs 0-63 (mesh 0) and over the threads on CPUs 64 and above (mesh 1) [Ref2]. The facts sheet prints them as "m0 + m1".

the field of a record that names its group of runs. Rerun at 7200 MT/s: `rerun-A`, `rerun-L`, `rerun-C`, `control-I`. Earlier run in the same 7200 MT/s boot: `F72d12`. 8000 MT/s runs of part A: `A-1`, `A-2`, `A-3`. 8000 MT/s runs of bwx12: `L-1` (the baseline with the identical argument line) and `L-2` to `L-4` (supporting rows). Runs of bwx11: `R0`, `R0b`. Runs of the first runner bwx: `B7a`, `B7b`, `C3a`, `C3b`. The facts sheet calls an earlier data set a "row", for example "row L-1". The records hold 8 more data sets, for example `X2d12` and three runs with 10 memory modules [Ref6]. This file selects none of them.
three constants of this file with data set names. `BW12` = L-1 to L-4 (runner bwx12). `BW11` = R0, R0b (runner bwx11). `BWX` = B7a, B7b, C3a, C3b (first runner bwx).
one bwx12 process with the argument line of part L. It ran on 2026-11-17 at 20:02 UTC in the same 7200 MT/s boot, before the rerun. It is not part of the rerun.

the field of a record that names its process or step. Rerun: the folder tag of the step, for example `T72A1` (part A, session 1), `T72L1` or `T72C4`. Earlier bwx runs: the name of the csv file without `.csv`, or the tag of the process inside the csv [Ref1].

bwx records: the kernel of the interval that ran directly before in the same process. For the first interval of a process the field holds the text `none (first interval of the process)`, which is the constant `FIRST` of this file. Part A records: binary and kernel of the process before it in the file. For the first process of a file the field holds the text `none (first process of the file)`. For the second and the third process of A-3 it holds a text that starts with `not listed`: other processes of `A3.csv` ran between the processes of A-3 [Ref1] [Ref2].
a text that names one process: folder, file, and process number or tag. The function `rng` counts the processes of a list with it.
the field `interval` of a record. Part A: the value of the column `rep` of the csv row (0, 1, 2). bwx runners: round x length of the kernel sequence + position.

the field `min_ms` of a record: the shortest length of one timed interval, in ms. Part A: 500 (0.5 s). `build_facts.py` writes this fixed value into every part A record [Ref1]. bwx runners: the value `min_ms` of the header line of the csv, 6000 (6 s) in the rerun.

the statistics object that `analyse` returns, a dictionary. `N['pa']`: the 6 pairs of part A. `N['pl']`, `N['pi']`, `N['pf']`, `N['pc']`, `N['p80']`: the pairs of the data sets `rerun-L`, `control-I`, `F72d12`, `rerun-C` and `L-1`. `N['pool']`: the selector function `pool`. `render` adds `N['CG']`, the five groups of part C.

six lists of drops in percent, one value per pair (lines 390 to 395). `dl`, `di` and `df` hold the drops of asmread in part L, in control I and in F72d12. `dcr` and `dca` hold the drops of `read` and of asmread in part C. `dpa` holds the drops of the 6 pairs of part A.

record lists that `render` selects at lines 414 to 421. `L72`, `I72`, `F72`, `A72` and `C72` are part L, control I, F72d12, part A and part C at 7200 MT/s. `P12` is the pool of the data sets L-1 to L-4 at 8000 MT/s. The last letter names the kernel: o = oldread (`bw_old read` in part A), a = asmread. `P12o` holds oldread at position 0 only. `P12a` holds asmread at position 1 only. Three more names follow the same pattern. `PALLo` and `PALLa` are these pools plus the bwx11 data sets R0 and R0b. `A80o` is `bw_old read` of the data sets A-1 to A-3.

the eight results of `compare` that `render` builds at lines 422 to 425. The second letter names the 7200 MT/s side: L = part L, I = control I, F = F72d12, A = part A, C = part C. The last letter names the kernel: o = the old read kernel (oldread, or `bw_old read` in part A), a = asmread. Each result holds `a` (the 7200 MT/s range), `b` (the 8000 MT/s range), `overlap`, `dist` (the distance of the nearest ends in GB/s), `wording` and `width`.
the verdict object, a dictionary. `render` returns it. `build_facts.py` stores it in facts.json under `verdicts`.
the text that answers Q1 or Q2 (`V['q1']`, `V['q2']`).
`L` is the list of the text lines of FACTS.md. `w` is a short name for `L.append`. One call `w(text)` adds one line. `L.extend(table(...))` adds the lines of one table.
the plain-text format of FACTS.md. A table row is one line with the cells between `|` characters.
Coordinated Universal Time, the time standard without a time zone offset. All times of the facts sheet are in UTC.
the time of the last change of a file, as the file system stores it. The Python function `os.path.getmtime` returns it.

inside `render`, `ref` is the object of the class `Refs` that `register` returns. `ref(path)` returns the text `[RefN]`. N is the number of that file in the file list of section 7 of the facts sheet. These numbers belong to the facts sheet. They are not the reference numbers of this page.

`ctx` is the dictionary that `render` passes to `section4` of facts_text4.py (line 1459). It holds the record lists and comparisons of this file. `section4` adds its own results to it, and `short_version` reads them under the name `c`. `extra` holds a few texts and values of section 1 that go into `ctx`.
a text with placeholders such as `%s`, `%d` or `%.2f`. The Python operator `%` puts values into the placeholders.
words that are written in a template of the source. No value from the data changes them.
a call `need(condition, text)`. The script stops with an error message when the condition is false.
a small Python function that is written as one expression, in the form `name = lambda arguments: expression`.
a fixed list of values in Python, written in round brackets.

two rates that are compared for Q1. Part A: the median of the bw_new process and the median of the bw_old process of the same session and round. bwx12: one interval of asmread or read, and the oldread interval of the same process and round.
(1 - new rate / old rate) x 100, in percent. It says how far the new read kernel or asmread is below the old read kernel.
the new rate divided by the old rate. It has no unit.

the middle value of a sorted list. For the 3 intervals of a part A process it is the second highest rate. For an even number of values the Python function `statistics.median` returns the mean of the two middle values.

the result of the function `rng` of facts_data.py for a list of records: the lowest rate `lo`, the highest rate `hi`, the median `med`, and the numbers of intervals `n`, of processes `procs`, of sessions `sessions` and of boots `boots` [Ref2].
of a range: (hi - lo) / lo x 100, in percent. For an 8000 MT/s range the facts sheet gives it as the size of a difference that the comparison cannot exclude (est.).

the fixed result text of rule V1 point 2 [Ref5]. The constant `SAME` is "no difference seen" (the two ranges overlap). The constant `DIFFERS` is "differs between the 8000 MT/s boot and the 7200 MT/s boot" (the two ranges do not overlap).
the two argument lines of part C. cfwd runs oldread, read, asmread. crev runs asmread, read, oldread.
a rounding rule: a value exactly in the middle between two steps is rounded to the step that is farther from 0. For a positive value that is the higher step.
the lettered list in section 2 of the facts sheet. Each entry is a choice that the author made for the run or for the analysis.
one entry of the list `detail` of `short_version`. The facts sheet prints the 12 detail lines as bullets under the three sentences of section 0.
one run of ra.sh or rx.sh in the rerun. It is one entry of `D['events']`, with the folder tag, the times, the load and the start state.
the first launch of a step minus the end of the previous 120-thread process of the rerun, in seconds.
a text per step. It says what ran before the first process of the step: an idle machine, or a 120-thread process that ended some seconds before.

one of the 27 checks of the raw files and scripts that the function `run_checks` of `build_facts.py` ran before `render` [Ref1]. Each check is one entry of the list `D['checks']` with a key (for example `sha-rx`), a result and a text. Section 1.4 of the facts sheet lists the checks.

files that the run scripts wrote into a result folder. probe.txt (ra.sh, part A): boot id, MemTotal, load, sha256 of bw_old, bw_new and ra.sh. env.txt (rx.sh): start time, Linux release, load, busiest processes, sha256 of bwx12. launches.txt (rx.sh): the launch line with load and arguments, and the rc line. stderr.txt: the error output of bwx12.
the record of the boot of the rerun. It holds the boot id, MemTotal, the Linux kernel message with the module count and the line with the memory speed 7200 MT/s.
the file `DIMM-flaky-report.md` (constant `DIMM_REPORT` of facts_data.py). It holds the boot history with the module count of each boot and the change of the memory speed to 7200 MT/s.

the list of boots in section 3 of the DIMM report, with the number, the start time and the module count of each boot. `D['boot_table']` holds it. `D['boot_table']` also holds the time until which the memory speed setting was 8000 MT/s.

files in `R/dimm-check-20261117`. h-1.txt and k-1.txt are the saved journal and the saved Linux kernel log of the 10-module boot that started on 2026-11-17 at 04:17 UTC. h-5.txt and k-5.txt are those of the 12-module boot in which the test of 2026-11-13 ran. That boot started on 2026-11-09.

a file in `R/dimm7200-20261117` that lists the boots of the journal: one row per boot with a number, the boot id and two times. Row 0 is the boot of try6.txt, which is the boot of the rerun. Its two times are 20:02:21 and 20:06:19 UTC on 2026-11-17. The second time equals the file time of boots.txt. So the row covers the boot only up to the moment when the file was written.
the file `S/baselines-and-rules.txt`: the fixed list of 8000 MT/s baselines and the comparison rules V1 to V4, F1 and F2. It was written before the run [Ref5].

a file in `S`. It holds the sha256 values that go.sh, ra.sh and the three spec files like.spec, cfwd.spec and crev.spec had when the rerun started. Line 20 of go.sh was edited on 2026-11-24. Since then go.sh no longer has the value that the file lists for it. The page `go.sh.md` in `S` (the explanation of go.sh) gives the record of the edit.
two earlier analysis scripts in `S`. They compute quick statistics of the part A files and of the bwx files. `build_facts.py` compares its own values with their output in two integrity checks [Ref1].
the part of the script of 2026-11-13 that ran 192 processes with one thread each. It ran after the build and the self-test, and before the 120-thread part.
`uefisettings`, a tool of Arm that reads and writes firmware settings. It needs root.
a file that the settings tool wrote. It holds a list of entries. Each entry has the name of a firmware setting, its answer (the value), its options and a help text.

a file that holds what the settings tool answered to a change of a setting. Each reply to a change carries the flag `modified`. Three of the four files (folders x1, x2 and revert) start with a date line. They also hold replies to readings of a setting, which carry no such flag.
the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
one DIMM. CRB has 12 slots.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the new read kernel or asmread.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
one pass of go.sh through part A, part L and part C.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the arguments of one bwx12 process, as a spec file holds them. "The same line" means a process with the same arguments.
a launch at a 1-minute load average below 1.0.
one time at which the same line was run. A later visit is the same line run again at a later time.
a line that go.sh or go2.sh prints with the time, the boot id, MemTotal, the load, the logins and the processes per user.

the row kinds of a bwx csv file: one I row per interval, one T row per thread and interval, one P row per thread before the first interval and after each interval (it holds the page state of the buffer), and one C row per thread and interval with counter values.
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.
the stop rule used with bwx12 here: all threads stop at the same time (after 6 s).

total_bytes / bytes_per_thread of an interval row of part A. For the kernels read and asmread this is the number of buffer passes that all 120 threads completed in the interval. The facts sheet prints a pass count for these two kernels only. For copy and asmcopy the same division gives 2 x the number of buffer passes, because the binary counts read plus written bytes (header line of each process in threads120.csv: "copy counts read+write bytes"). facts.json holds that value in the field "passes".
part A: the column aggregate_GBps that bandwidth.c prints. bwx runners: the sum over the threads of bytes / elapsed time. Unit GB/s.

the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (file /proc/loadavg). "Load at launch" is the 1-minute value read directly before a process starts. The fourth field of the file gives the tasks that are runnable now and the number of all tasks.

the column pcpu of the tool ps in the process lists of env.txt and probe.txt. It is the CPU time that a process has used, divided by the time since the process started. So it is an average over the life of the process. It is not the use at the moment of the reading.
a Linux kernel thread in the process lists. By its name it prints kernel messages to the serial console ttyAMA. This meaning was not checked on CRB.
a random identifier that Linux creates at each start. Equal boot ids mean the same boot.
the usable memory that Linux reports, in kB.
2^30 bytes. A "32 GB" module holds 32 GiB.
2^20 bytes. The buffer of one thread is 256 MiB.

the output of the command `dmidecode -t 17`, which prints the hardware table of the firmware. It holds one entry "Memory Device" per memory module: 12 entries in the list saved in the boot of the rerun, and 10 entries in a 10-module boot by the DIMM report.
the log store of Linux. It keeps the kernel log of earlier boots.

a message that the firmware passes to Linux when hardware reports an error. Linux prints it in the kernel log with the tag "[Hardware Error]". Its severity is "corrected" (the hardware repaired it) or "recoverable" (not repaired, the system continues).

firmware settings that limit the read requests of the cores. They are not memory settings. The saved replies of the settings tool name two of them: "TXREQ Max" and "TXREQ Min" (section 1.5, point 13 of the facts sheet).
transparent huge pages. The "P" rows of bwx12 report how many kB of each buffer lie on them.
`/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. Another user creates it during a performance test. Our scripts stop when it exists.
the Linux policy that sets the CPU frequency.
the exit status of a process. 0 means success.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
an earlier 8000 MT/s run with 12 modules that used the same binary and method as a part of the rerun. The list was fixed before the run.
earlier 8000 MT/s runs that differ in interval length or counter setup (supporting), or that used another runner binary (other binary).
two min-to-max ranges share at least one value.
the number of measurements that a range comes from. It is written as intervals / processes / sessions / boots (rule V1 point 1). "No session" marks a row that is not part of a session of go.sh.
the intervals of several rows taken together as one range.
for two ranges that do not overlap: the lowest value of the higher range minus the highest value of the lower range.

words.term: Rules V1 to V4, F1, F2
words.def: the comparison rules in `baselines-and-rules.txt`.
the facts sheet of the investigation of 2026-11-15 into the drop of the read rate.
estimated, not measured directly.
